name: tar
description: Tape ARchiver: bundles many files into one archive, optionally compressed. The mnemonic: Create, eXtract, List.

flags.description: Archive filename (almost always required, comes last in short flags).
Filter through gzip / bzip2 / xz compression.
Change to DIR before operating (extract target).

examples.explanation: Creates a gzip-compressed archive of the project directory. c=create, z=gzip, f=filename.
Extracts into the current directory. Modern tar auto-detects compression: tar -xf backup.tar.gz also works.
Lists the first entries WITHOUT extracting — always inspect unknown archives first.
Extracts into a specific existing directory instead of the current one.
Archives a web project while skipping dependencies and version-control data.

about: tar preserves Unix metadata: permissions, ownership (as root), timestamps, and symlinks. Compression is a filter, not a feature of tar itself — .tar.gz (gzip: fast), .tar.bz2 (better ratio), .tar.xz (best ratio, slowest). GNU tar auto-detects the compression of input archives when extracting.
useCases: Transferring many files as one unit.
mistakes: Forgetting -f (or putting it before other flags): tar czf file.tar.gz works, tar -fz file.tar.gz does not.
Extracting unknown archives in the current directory and scattering files — list first with -t.
Double extensions missing: file.tar.gz must be created with -z, file.tar without.
warnings: Never extract archives as root without inspecting them: malicious archives can contain absolute paths or ../ traversals (path traversal). GNU tar strips leading / by default but verify with -t.
distroNotes: GNU tar is universal on Linux. BSD tar (bsdtar) shares the common flags; GNU extensions like --transform are not portable.
